title: Shortest path through the warehouse
statement:
A warehouse floor is a grid where 0 is an open aisle and 1 is a shelf. A robot starts at the top-left cell and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving up, down, left or right one cell per step through open cells only.

Return the fewest steps needed, or -1 if it cannot get there. If the start or end is a shelf, return -1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which moves are allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up, down, left and right, one cell per step.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the start or end is a shelf?
What if start and end are the same cell?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: For a 1 by 1 open grid, return 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is the grid?
clarifyingQuestions.why: BFS over all cells is fine.

hiddenConstraints: The grid has at least one cell.

edgeCases.why: BFS must find the shortest, not the first path DFS finds.

approaches.name: DFS over all paths
approaches.idea: Explore every path and keep the shortest.
approaches.tradeoffs: Far too slow, and DFS’s first path is not the shortest.

approaches.name: Breadth-first search
approaches.idea: BFS explores cells in order of distance from the start, so the first time it reaches the end is the shortest path.

optimal.name: BFS from the start
optimal.explanation: Return -1 if start or end is blocked. Queue the start with distance 0 and mark it seen. Pop cells in order; if it is the end, return its distance. Otherwise push each open, unseen, in-bounds neighbor with distance + 1, marking it seen when pushed. If the queue empties, return -1.

hintLadder: Does every step cost the same?
Which traversal reaches cells in order of distance?
How do you avoid visiting a cell twice?
Run BFS from the start, marking cells when you enqueue them, and return the distance when you reach the end.

expectedMentions.what: Asks what to do if the start or end is blocked
Explains why BFS gives the shortest path with equal step costs
Proposes BFS with O(rows * cols) time before coding
Marks cells as seen when enqueued to avoid duplicates
Traces the example or the unreachable case

followUps: The robot may remove one shelf. What is the new shortest path?
Steps through some aisles cost more. What changes?

walkthrough.say: Only four directions, one cell per step? If the start or the end is a shelf, I return minus one? And a one-cell open grid is zero steps?
Every step costs the same, so breadth-first search finds the shortest path: it reaches all cells at distance d before any at distance d plus one. Each cell is visited once, so O(rows times cols).
DFS would find a path but not necessarily the shortest one, so it’s the wrong tool here.
Check the blocked cases first, then BFS with the distance stored alongside each cell.
Marking cells when I enqueue them means no cell enters the queue twice.
For the example: start at the top left, right to column 1, down twice through column 1, then right to the corner. That’s 4 steps, and BFS finds it at distance 4.
For 0, 1 over 1, 0, the start’s neighbors are both shelves, so the queue empties and I return minus one.
O(rows times cols) time and space. With different step costs I’d switch to Dijkstra’s algorithm.
